disease.name: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD)
disease.scientific_name: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease / Gastro-Oesophageal Reflux Disease (GORD)
disease.icd_10_code: K21 (Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease); K21.0 (GERD with oesophagitis); K21.9 (GERD without oesophagitis); K22.1 (Ulcer of oesophagus); K22.2 (Oesophageal obstruction); C15 (Malignant neoplasm of oesophagus — late complication)

overview.description: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) is a chronic, relapsing digestive condition in which the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) fails to prevent the retrograde flow of gastric contents — acid, pepsin, bile salts, and pancreatic enzymes — from the stomach back into the esophagus, causing troublesome symptoms and/or complications. The hallmark symptoms are heartburn (a retrosternal burning sensation) and acid regurgitation (sour or bitter taste in the mouth). GERD exists on a spectrum from non-erosive reflux disease (NERD — symptoms without visible mucosal damage) to erosive esophagitis, Barrett's esophagus, and in a minority, esophageal adenocarcinoma. It is one of the most prevalent gastrointestinal conditions globally, significantly impairing quality of life and imposing substantial economic burden through medication costs and healthcare utilisation.
overview.affected_organ: Esophagus (primary); also pharynx, larynx, lungs, oral cavity in extraesophageal GERD
overview.prevalence: One of the most common GI conditions globally — prevalence ~20% in North America and Europe; 10-20% in South America; 5-10% in Asia (increasing with Westernisation of diet and lifestyle). Affects an estimated 1 billion people worldwide.
overview.age_group: All age groups affected; highest symptomatic prevalence in adults 40-60 years; increasing in elderly; GERD in infants is physiological and usually resolves; alarming rise in paediatric and obese adolescent populations.
overview.key_fact: GERD is the most common cause of non-cardiac chest pain; up to 30% of 'cardiac chest pain' investigations ultimately prove to be GERD-related

anatomy_and_pathophysiology_overview.lower_esophageal_sphincter: The LES is a 3-4 cm high-pressure zone at the gastroesophageal junction (GEJ) maintained by intrinsic smooth muscle tone, diaphragmatic crural contraction (external sphincter), and the angle of His (acute angle between esophagus and stomach). Normal resting LES pressure: 10-45 mmHg. LES pressure <10 mmHg (hypotensive LES) allows reflux.
anatomy_and_pathophysiology_overview.primary_mechanism: Transient Lower Esophageal Sphincter Relaxations (TLESRs) — inappropriate, prolonged relaxations of the LES not triggered by swallowing — are the primary mechanism in 90% of GERD patients. Mediated by vagal reflex involving GABA-B and mGluR5 receptors (target of baclofen therapy). TLESRs allow acid pockets (accumulated in the fundus) to reflux into the esophagus.
secondary_mechanisms: Hypotensive LES (persistently low resting pressure) — allows free reflux; associated with scleroderma, advanced GERD
Hiatal hernia — displaces acid pocket above the diaphragm; impairs crural compression of LES; reduces esophageal acid clearance
Impaired esophageal acid clearance — reduced peristaltic amplitude; reduced salivary bicarbonate secretion
Delayed gastric emptying — increases intragastric volume and pressure promoting reflux
Increased gastric acid secretion — amplifies mucosal damage when reflux occurs
Impaired mucosal defense — weakened esophageal epithelial barrier from chronic acid exposure
anatomy_and_pathophysiology_overview.acid_pocket: After meals, an 'acid pocket' forms in the proximal stomach just below the gastroesophageal junction — a reservoir of unbuffered acid that is the source of post-prandial reflux. Hiatal hernias displace the acid pocket above the diaphragm, making it immediately accessible to the esophagus during TLESRs.

types.name: Non-Erosive Reflux Disease (NERD)
types.description: The most common GERD phenotype — accounting for 60-70% of all GERD patients. Classic heartburn and regurgitation symptoms WITHOUT visible mucosal damage (normal or near-normal endoscopy). Not a 'milder' form — NERD patients have equivalent symptom severity and quality of life impairment to erosive esophagitis. Mechanisms: visceral hypersensitivity (increased sensitivity of esophageal sensory afferents), microscopic mucosal changes not visible macroscopically, and abnormal acid exposure.
types.endoscopy: Normal or near-normal mucosal appearance (no erosions, no visible lesions)
types.response_to_PPI: 50-60% symptom response (lower than erosive esophagitis) — some patients have functional heartburn overlapping
types.common_in: Women slightly more than men; all ages
types.note: Despite normal endoscopy, abnormal acid exposure is demonstrated on pH monitoring in ~50%; remaining 50% may have hypersensitive esophagus or functional heartburn

types.name: Erosive Esophagitis (EE) — Reflux Esophagitis
types.description: GERD with macroscopically visible mucosal breaks (erosions or ulcers) in the esophageal mucosa on endoscopy. Graded by the Los Angeles (LA) Classification System. More common in men, obese individuals, and those with hiatal hernia. Higher rates of complications (stricture, Barrett's) than NERD. Typically responds well to PPI therapy (90% healing at 8 weeks).

la_classification.grade_A: One or more mucosal breaks ≤5mm in maximum length
la_classification.grade_B: One or more mucosal breaks >5mm in maximum length, not continuous between the tops of two mucosal folds
la_classification.grade_C: Mucosal breaks continuous between the tops of two or more mucosal folds but involving less than 75% of the esophageal circumference
la_classification.grade_D: Mucosal breaks involving ≥75% of the esophageal circumference (severe — highest risk of complications)

types.common_in: Men; obese; hiatal hernia; severe GERD
types.healing: 90% heal with 8 weeks of standard-dose PPI; 100% with higher-dose or longer course

types.name: Barrett's Esophagus
types.description: A pre-malignant complication of chronic GERD in which the normal stratified squamous epithelium of the distal esophagus is replaced by specialised intestinal metaplasia (columnar epithelium with goblet cells) — the body's adaptive response to chronic acid injury. Barrett's is the most significant risk factor for esophageal adenocarcinoma — which has one of the fastest rising incidence rates of any cancer in Western countries.
types.prevalence: Occurs in ~10-15% of patients with chronic GERD; affects 1-2% of general adult population
types.cancer_risk: Annual risk of progression to esophageal adenocarcinoma: ~0.3% per year; increases with dysplasia (low-grade: ~0.5%/year; high-grade: 6-7%/year)
types.risk_factors: Male sex, age >50, central obesity, long duration of GERD (>5 years), hiatal hernia, family history of Barrett's or esophageal cancer, smoking, Caucasian ethnicity
types.management: Surveillance endoscopy every 3-5 years (no dysplasia); annual (low-grade dysplasia); endoscopic eradication therapy (radiofrequency ablation — RFA; cryotherapy) for dysplastic Barrett's; esophagectomy for T1N0 cancer in selected cases

types.name: Extraesophageal GERD (Laryngopharyngeal Reflux — LPR)
types.description: GERD manifestations beyond the esophagus — occurring in the larynx, pharynx, lungs, nasal passages, and oral cavity. Refluxate reaches the larynx and pharynx either by direct proximal extension or by vagal reflex-mediated mechanisms. Often presents WITHOUT typical heartburn ('silent reflux') — making diagnosis challenging. More common than traditionally recognised.
common_manifestations: Laryngopharyngeal reflux (LPR): hoarseness, chronic throat clearing, globus sensation (lump in throat), sore throat
Reflux-associated chronic cough: persistent non-productive cough — GERD accounts for 20-40% of cases
Reflux-associated asthma: GERD can trigger or worsen bronchospasm
Dental erosion: acid contacts teeth during nighttime reflux episodes
Laryngeal cancer risk (acid contact with laryngeal mucosa)
types.diagnosis: More challenging — ambulatory pH-impedance with dual sensors (distal + proximal esophageal); laryngoscopy showing posterior laryngeal erythema and swelling (Reflux Finding Score)
types.treatment: Requires higher PPI doses (twice daily); longer treatment courses (3-6 months); lifestyle changes especially crucial (positional)

types.name: Refractory GERD
types.description: Persistent symptoms despite standard PPI therapy (once-daily PPI for 8 weeks). Affects approximately 30-40% of GERD patients. Causes: non-adherence to PPI dosing (most common — PPI must be taken 30-60 min before meals); weakly acidic or non-acid reflux; functional heartburn (central sensitisation without true reflux); bile reflux; delayed gastric emptying; NERD with visceral hypersensitivity; PPI malabsorption (CYP2C19 rapid metabolisers).
types.evaluation: pH-impedance monitoring ON PPI therapy (identifies weakly acidic or non-acid reflux); symptom-reflux association analysis; esophageal manometry; gastric emptying study
types.management: Optimise PPI timing and dose; pH-impedance guided; add-on agents (alginate, prokinetic, baclofen for non-acid reflux); consider laparoscopic fundoplication for non-acid refractory GERD; neuromodulators (TCA, SSRI) for functional heartburn

types.name: Hypersensitive Esophagus
types.description: A subset of NERD — patients have normal acid exposure on pH testing but symptoms are triggered by physiologically normal amounts of acid because of heightened esophageal sensory threshold (visceral hypersensitivity). Symptoms are temporally correlated with normal reflux events on pH monitoring (positive symptom-reflux association index). Central and peripheral sensitisation mechanisms involved.
types.management: PPIs have limited efficacy; neuromodulators (tricyclic antidepressants, SSRIs, SNRIs) reduce visceral hypersensitivity; psychological therapies (CBT, hypnotherapy for gut-brain axis); gabapentin
types.distinction: Important to distinguish from true acid GERD — different management pathway; PPI escalation is not beneficial

types.name: Functional Heartburn
types.description: Rome IV functional esophageal disorder — heartburn symptoms with NORMAL pH testing and NO correlation between symptoms and reflux events on pH-impedance monitoring. Part of the spectrum of functional gastrointestinal disorders (similar to IBS). Mechanisms: abnormal central pain processing; psychological factors (anxiety, depression, catastrophising); esophageal hypersensitivity.
types.management: Reassurance and explanation; PPIs generally ineffective; neuromodulators (antidepressants) effective; CBT; gut-directed hypnotherapy; address anxiety and stress
types.note: Important diagnosis to make to avoid long-term unnecessary PPI therapy and escalation to surgery

types.name: Alkaline / Bile Reflux
types.description: Reflux of duodenal contents (bile, pancreatic enzymes) into the esophagus — either alone or mixed with gastric acid. Bile salts cause mucosal injury independent of acid. More common post-gastrectomy or Billroth surgery. Can cause GERD symptoms that do not respond to PPIs (since PPIs reduce acid but not bile). Detected by impedance monitoring or bilirubin sensor (Bilitec).
types.management: Prokinetics; cholestyramine (bile acid binder); alginate barriers; surgical correction (Roux-en-Y diversion) in severe post-surgical bile reflux; GERD surgery

severity_levels.name: Mild GERD
severity_levels.description: Infrequent, mild heartburn with minimal impact on daily life
severity_levels.frequency: Heartburn ≤1-2 days per week; episodes brief
severity_levels.symptom_severity: Mild burning discomfort; easily relieved by antacids
severity_levels.quality_of_life: Minimal impairment; able to eat and sleep normally
severity_levels.endoscopy: Normal or Grade A erosive esophagitis
severity_levels.management: Lifestyle modifications; antacids or alginates as needed (PRN); consider H2 blocker for persistent symptoms; OTC PPI short course
severity_levels.monitoring: Annual symptom review; no urgent investigations required unless alarm symptoms

severity_levels.name: Moderate GERD
severity_levels.description: Frequent symptoms affecting daily activities and quality of life
severity_levels.frequency: Heartburn 2-4 days per week; nocturnal symptoms
severity_levels.symptom_severity: Moderate heartburn and regurgitation; partially relieved by antacids but requiring regular medication
severity_levels.quality_of_life: Significant — affects eating, sleep, and social activities
severity_levels.endoscopy: Grade A-B erosive esophagitis or NERD
severity_levels.management: Standard-dose PPI (omeprazole 20mg or equivalent) once daily before breakfast for 4-8 weeks; lifestyle modifications; step-down to maintenance H2 blocker or on-demand PPI if responding
severity_levels.monitoring: Endoscopy if symptoms persist >8 weeks on PPI or alarm features develop

severity_levels.name: Severe / Complicated GERD
severity_levels.description: Frequent severe symptoms with complications or resistant to standard therapy
severity_levels.frequency: Daily symptoms; nocturnal heartburn; significant regurgitation
severity_levels.symptom_severity: Severe heartburn, regurgitation, dysphagia; sleep disturbance; extraesophageal symptoms
severity_levels.quality_of_life: Severely impaired; avoidance of meals; significant impact on employment and social life
severity_levels.endoscopy: Grade C-D erosive esophagitis; peptic stricture; suspected or confirmed Barrett's esophagus
severity_levels.management: Double-dose PPI (omeprazole 20mg twice daily or equivalent); prokinetics; surgical evaluation; Barrett's surveillance protocol; dilatation if peptic stricture
severity_levels.monitoring: Repeat endoscopy at 4-8 weeks on high-dose PPI; Barrett's surveillance; pH-impedance if refractory

severity_levels.name: GERD with Barrett's Esophagus or Dysplasia
severity_levels.description: GERD complicated by Barrett's esophagus ± dysplasia — highest risk category requiring specialist gastroenterology/oncology management
severity_levels.symptoms: May have severe or minimal GERD symptoms; symptoms may paradoxically reduce once columnar metaplasia established (less acid-sensitive mucosa)
severity_levels.risk: Barrett's without dysplasia: 0.3%/year cancer risk; Low-grade dysplasia: 0.5%/year; High-grade dysplasia: 6-7%/year
severity_levels.management: High-dose PPI (acid suppression protective); Barrett's surveillance endoscopy program; endoscopic eradication therapy (radiofrequency ablation for dysplastic Barrett's); multidisciplinary team (MDT) decision for surgery vs endoscopic management in dysplasia
severity_levels.monitoring: Structured Barrett's surveillance protocol per BSG/ACG/AGA guidelines

transient_LES_relaxations.description: TLESRs are the predominant mechanism of GERD (responsible for 90% of reflux episodes). These are abrupt, inappropriate relaxations of the lower esophageal sphincter occurring independently of swallowing, lasting 10-45 seconds (vs 6-8 seconds for swallow-induced relaxations). Triggered by: gastric distension (especially fundal distension after meals), fatty meals, air swallowing, and vagal nerve stimulation.
transient_LES_relaxations.pharmacological_target: GABA-B receptors and mGluR5 receptors mediate TLESRs — targeted by baclofen (GABA-B agonist) to reduce TLESR frequency

primary_mechanism.hypotensive_LES: Chronically low resting LES pressure (<6 mmHg) allows free reflux independent of TLESRs; associated with scleroderma, severe GERD, obesity; most significant when combined with hiatal hernia
primary_mechanism.hiatal_hernia: Displacement of the gastric cardia above the diaphragmatic hiatus disrupts the anti-reflux barrier: (1) Separates the crural diaphragm (external sphincter) from the LES; (2) Moves the acid pocket above the diaphragm; (3) Reduces LES pressure; (4) Impairs esophageal acid clearance via hernial 'acid trap'

predisposing_conditions.mechanism: Increased intra-abdominal pressure compresses the stomach, promoting reflux; excess visceral fat increases intragastric pressure; disrupts gastroesophageal junction anatomy; promotes hiatal hernia; adipokines alter LES function. BMI >30: 3-4x increased GERD risk; each 5-unit BMI increase raises GERD risk by 35%
predisposing_conditions.category: Modifiable — Weight loss is most evidence-based intervention

predisposing_conditions.mechanism: Structural defect at GEJ — see above; found in >80% of patients with severe erosive esophagitis; accelerates disease progression
Prolonged retention of gastric contents increases intragastric volume and acid exposure time; promotes distension-triggered TLESRs; common in diabetes, post-vagotomy, connective tissue disease
Progesterone reduces LES pressure; mechanical displacement of stomach by growing uterus increases intra-abdominal pressure; affects 30-80% of pregnant women — most severe in 3rd trimester
Scleroderma/systemic sclerosis causes fibrosis of esophageal smooth muscle — severe LES hypotension and impaired esophageal peristalsis; one of the most challenging GERD cases

dietary_triggers.mechanism: Directly reduce LES pressure via CCK-mediated vagal reflex; delay gastric emptying; large caloric load distends the stomach
Directly relaxes LES smooth muscle; stimulates gastric acid secretion; promotes TLESRs
Contains methylxanthines (caffeine, theobromine) that relax LES; also high fat content; increases TLESRs
L-menthol directly relaxes LES smooth muscle (calcium channel-dependent); despite perceived GI benefit, worsens GERD
Reduces LES pressure; stimulates gastric acid secretion; impairs esophageal peristalsis (impaired clearance); directly damages esophageal mucosa
Directly lower pH in stomach and esophagus; may worsen existing mucosal damage even without increasing reflux volume
examples: Citrus fruits and juices (orange, lemon, grapefruit)
Tomatoes and tomato products (passata, ketchup, pizza sauce)

dietary_triggers.mechanism: Capsaicin activates TRPV1 receptors on esophageal afferent nerves, increasing pain perception; may irritate already-inflamed mucosa; delays gastric emptying
Fermentable carbohydrates cause gas production and gastric distension; increase TLESRs; raw form more provocative than cooked
CO2 gas distends the stomach, directly triggering TLESRs; acid content worsens mucosal injury

medications_causing_gerd.mechanism: Inhibit COX-1 reducing prostaglandin-mediated mucosal protection; cause direct mucosal injury (topical irritant); may reduce LES pressure; cause gastric erosions and exacerbate reflux

medications_causing_gerd.medication: Calcium Channel Blockers (amlodipine, nifedipine, verapamil, diltiazem)
medications_causing_gerd.mechanism: Relax LES smooth muscle (calcium-dependent contraction); reduce LES pressure significantly
Nitric oxide-mediated LES relaxation; reduce LES pressure
Reduce LES pressure and esophageal peristalsis; delay gastric emptying
Direct chemical injury to esophageal mucosa if taken incorrectly (must be taken with large volume of water and remain upright for 30 minutes); cause severe pill-induced esophagitis
Reduces LES pressure; stimulates acid secretion; used in COPD/asthma — important drug-disease interaction
Reduce LES pressure; delay gastric emptying; impair esophageal peristalsis
Pill-induced esophagitis — direct mucosal injury from prolonged contact if not taken with adequate water and upright posture

risk_factors: Obesity (BMI >25) — especially central/visceral obesity; strongest modifiable risk factor
Smoking — reduces LES pressure; impairs salivary bicarbonate; increases acid output; impairs esophageal motility
Age >40 years — increased hiatal hernia prevalence; reduced esophageal clearance efficiency
Male sex — higher rates of erosive esophagitis and Barrett's; females more symptomatic with NERD
Sedentary lifestyle — reduces gut motility; promotes obesity
Large meals, eating quickly, eating late at night
Wearing tight belts and clothing compressing abdomen
Psychological stress and anxiety — increases acid sensitivity and visceral hypersensitivity
Sleep apnoea — associated with nocturnal GERD (bidirectional relationship)
Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (rare — gastrinoma causing massive acid hypersecretion)
Family history — genetic predisposition to LES dysfunction and GERD

primary_symptoms.name: Heartburn (Pyrosis)
primary_symptoms.description: The cardinal symptom of GERD — a burning, uncomfortable sensation rising from the epigastrium (upper abdomen) up behind the breastbone (substernal) and sometimes into the throat. Often described as 'acid rising', 'burning in chest', 'fire in chest' or 'heat in the throat'. Typically occurs 30-60 minutes after meals, on bending forward, or lying down. May radiate to the throat or jaw. Worsens with trigger foods, alcohol, and large meals. Classically relieved by antacids (diagnostic).
primary_symptoms.onset: Post-prandial (30-60 min after meals); nocturnal; on bending or lying
primary_symptoms.distinguishing_feature: Relief with antacids is highly specific for acid-related disease; positional worsening (bending, lying) distinguishes from cardiac angina
primary_symptoms.note: Heartburn occurring >2 days/week for >4-8 weeks = GERD by definition (Montréal Consensus)

primary_symptoms.name: Acid Regurgitation
primary_symptoms.description: The passive, effortless return of gastric contents (sour, bitter, or acidic liquid, partially digested food, or bile) into the esophagus, pharynx, and mouth — without nausea or retching (distinguishing it from vomiting). The second most specific symptom of GERD. Patients describe a 'sour or bitter taste in the mouth', 'fluid rising into the throat', or 'burping up acid'. Worsens on bending forward, lying down, and during increased abdominal pressure (coughing, straining).
primary_symptoms.onset: Post-prandial and nocturnal; on positional change

primary_symptoms.name: Dysphagia (Difficulty Swallowing)
primary_symptoms.description: Sensation of food or liquid sticking in the esophagus during or after swallowing. In GERD, dysphagia results from: (1) Peptic esophageal stricture (fibrotic narrowing from chronic acid injury); (2) Severe esophageal inflammation (grade C-D esophagitis); (3) Esophageal dysmotility from chronic acid exposure. Dysphagia is an ALARM SYMPTOM — always requires urgent endoscopy to exclude malignancy. Progressive dysphagia (solids first, then liquids) is more concerning for stricture or malignancy.
primary_symptoms.warning: NEW ONSET DYSPHAGIA IS AN ALARM SYMPTOM — always requires urgent endoscopy to exclude malignancy

primary_symptoms.name: Regurgitation and Waterbrash
primary_symptoms.description: Waterbrash is the sudden appearance of large amounts of thin, salty, clear fluid in the mouth — caused by excessive salivation (hypersalivation) in response to esophageal or gastric acid stimulation of a vagal reflex. Distinct from regurgitation (which produces acidic fluid). A classic but underrecognised GERD symptom. Patients often awaken at night with mouth full of clear, dilute, slightly salty fluid.

primary_symptoms.name: Chest Pain (Non-Cardiac)
primary_symptoms.description: Retrosternal (chest) pain from esophageal acid exposure, esophageal spasm triggered by acid, or visceral hypersensitivity. Can be indistinguishable from cardiac angina — substernal, may radiate to arm or jaw. GERD accounts for 20-30% of non-cardiac chest pain investigations. Responds to PPI trial (diagnostic and therapeutic). ALWAYS exclude cardiac cause FIRST before attributing chest pain to GERD.
primary_symptoms.note: CARDIAC CHEST PAIN MUST ALWAYS BE EXCLUDED FIRST — never assume chest pain is GERD without cardiac evaluation

primary_symptoms.name: Odynophagia (Painful Swallowing)
primary_symptoms.description: Pain when food or liquid passes through the esophagus during swallowing — usually substernal. Suggests active mucosal inflammation (severe erosive esophagitis, esophageal ulcer) or pill-induced esophagitis. Odynophagia with dysphagia is a double alarm sign requiring urgent endoscopy.
primary_symptoms.warning: Odynophagia combined with dysphagia is a double alarm symptom — urgent endoscopy required

secondary_symptoms: Belching and bloating — gastric distension from air swallowing (aerophagia) and impaired gastric emptying; triggers TLESRs
Nausea — especially in the morning (nocturnal reflux reaching pharynx/larynx); may rarely cause vomiting
Epigastric pain and discomfort — upper abdominal burning or fullness (overlap with functional dyspepsia — Montréal Consensus recognises dyspeptic-GERD overlap)
Early satiety and postprandial fullness — delayed gastric emptying component
Globus sensation — feeling of a lump or tightness in the throat without true swallowing difficulty; common in LPR
Throat clearing and cough — from LPR (posterior laryngeal irritation) or cough reflex from esophageal-bronchial reflex
Hoarseness and voice changes — morning hoarseness from overnight acid laryngeal irritation; contact ulcers; vocal cord nodules in chronic LPR
Dental erosion — loss of tooth enamel from repeated acid contact; particularly affecting palatal surfaces of maxillary incisors
Chronic sore throat — posterior pharyngeal and laryngeal acid irritation
Hiccups — diaphragmatic irritation from acid at GEJ
Excessive mucus in throat — secretory response to laryngeal acid irritation
Coughing or choking when lying down — aspiration of refluxate into airways (nocturnal)
Halitosis (bad breath) — from acid in mouth and upper GI tract

alarm_symptoms_red_flags.description: The following symptoms in a patient with GERD or heartburn require URGENT investigation (typically endoscopy) to exclude malignancy, serious pathology, or complicated GERD. These should NOT be managed empirically with PPIs alone.
flags: Progressive dysphagia (difficulty swallowing that is worsening) — possible esophageal stricture or malignancy
Odynophagia (painful swallowing) — possible ulceration, malignancy, or infectious esophagitis
Unintentional weight loss (>5% body weight over 3-6 months) — possible malignancy
Persistent vomiting — possible outlet obstruction or malignancy
Evidence of GI bleeding: haematemesis (vomiting blood), melaena (black tarry stools), iron-deficiency anaemia
New onset symptoms in age >55 years — higher risk of malignancy
Family history of upper GI cancer
alarm_symptoms_red_flags.urgency: 2-week wait urgent endoscopy referral for most alarm features (UK NICE guidelines); emergency endoscopy if active bleeding

infants: Physiological GER (gastroesophageal reflux) is NORMAL in infants — affects up to 50% of infants under 3 months (due to horizontal posture, liquid diet, immature LES, short esophagus, relatively larger gastric volume)
Most infant reflux resolves spontaneously by 12-18 months when the infant becomes upright and starts solids

Symptoms: frequent spitting up/vomiting (regurgitation) after feeds; arching of back during or after feeds (Sandifer syndrome — dystonic posturing); feeding refusal; irritability; poor weight gain; recurrent respiratory symptoms (aspiration)
Distinguish from pyloric stenosis: projectile non-bilious vomiting in first 6 weeks of life (earlier, more forceful, olive-shaped mass)
older_children: May report heartburn and regurgitation (similar to adults) from age 8-10 onwards
Abdominal pain and non-cardiac chest pain
Dental erosion (dentist often first to notice)
School avoidance and reduced quality of life from chronic symptoms

diagnostic_approach.clinical_diagnosis: In uncomplicated patients under 55 years with typical heartburn and regurgitation and NO alarm symptoms, GERD can be diagnosed clinically without investigations — empirical PPI trial is both diagnostic and therapeutic.
diagnostic_approach.empirical_ppi_trial: Standard-dose PPI (omeprazole 20mg) before breakfast for 4-8 weeks; symptomatic response supports GERD diagnosis; sensitivity ~75%, specificity ~55% for GERD — not definitive
investigation_indications: Symptoms not responding to 8 weeks of standard PPI

medical_history: Detailed symptom characterisation: heartburn (location, quality, radiation, timing — post-prandial, nocturnal, positional), regurgitation frequency, dysphagia (solids/liquids/both), odynophagia
Symptom duration, frequency, and progression over time
Relationship to specific foods, meals, posture, exercise
Previous endoscopy results and Barrett's diagnosis
Current medications: NSAIDs, calcium channel blockers, nitrates, bisphosphonates, anticholinergics
Past medical history: hiatal hernia, obesity, diabetes, scleroderma, previous GI surgery
Family history: esophageal or gastric cancer, Barrett's esophagus
Dietary history: caffeine, alcohol, high-fat diet intake, meal timing
Lifestyle: smoking, alcohol, BMI, physical activity, sleep position
Previous treatment response: antacids, H2RAs, PPIs — response and current adherence
Psychological history: anxiety and depression (visceral hypersensitivity, functional overlap)
physical_examination: BMI and abdominal girth measurement — central obesity is a key modifiable risk factor
Abdominal examination: epigastric tenderness (peptic ulcer, esophagitis); palpable epigastric mass (rare — malignancy); hepatomegaly

Throat and larynx examination (or ENT referral): posterior laryngeal erythema, interarytenoid oedema, vocal cord contact ulcers, posterior pharyngeal wall cobblestoning (LPR signs — Reflux Finding Score >7)
Oral examination: dental erosion on palatal surfaces of maxillary teeth (pathognomonic for chronic acid contact — dentist may refer)
Respiratory examination: wheeze or prolonged expiratory phase (reflux-associated asthma)
Chest auscultation: aspiration-related crackles (rare); signs of aspiration pneumonia
Skin and joint examination: telangiectasia, sclerodactyly, Raynaud's (scleroderma — associated with severe GERD)

diagnostic_tests.description: Gold standard for visualising esophageal mucosa, diagnosing complications, and obtaining biopsies. Allows direct grading of erosive esophagitis (LA classification), identification and biopsy of Barrett's esophagus, detection of peptic stricture, hiatal hernia assessment, and exclusion of malignancy. An ESSENTIAL investigation whenever alarm symptoms are present.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose complications (erosive esophagitis, Barrett's, peptic stricture, malignancy); grade severity; guide management; screen for Barrett's in high-risk patients
diagnostic_tests.indications: Alarm symptoms; age >55 new onset; failed PPI response; before antireflux surgery; Barrett's surveillance; suspected complications
key_findings: Normal: supports NERD or functional heartburn
LA Grade A-D esophagitis: confirms erosive GERD
Barrett's esophagus (salmon-coloured tongue of mucosa proximal to GEJ — Prague criteria for length)
Hiatal hernia (gastric cardia herniated above diaphragm)
Peptic stricture (smooth narrowing of distal esophagus)

diagnostic_tests.description: Gold standard for quantifying esophageal acid exposure. A thin pH probe is passed transnasally and positioned 5cm above the LES manometrically. Records esophageal pH continuously for 24 hours during normal activities. Patient records meals, posture changes, and symptoms. Calculates DeMeester score (composite score — normal <14.72), acid exposure time (AET — normal <4%), number of reflux episodes, symptom-reflux association (SAP and SI).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm abnormal acid exposure in GERD; correlate symptoms with reflux events; assess refractory GERD ON PPI therapy; pre-surgical evaluation
diagnostic_tests.when_to_perform: Off PPI: confirm GERD diagnosis in equivocal cases; On PPI: evaluate refractory GERD (determines if symptoms correlate with breakthrough reflux)
diagnostic_tests.key_metrics: AET >4%: abnormal (6%: severe); DeMeester score >14.72: abnormal; SAP >95% or SI >50%: positive symptom-reflux association
diagnostic_tests.patient_instruction: Stop PPIs 7 days before test (H2RAs 3 days); eat normally; record symptoms, meals, posture in diary

diagnostic_tests.description: Combined pH and multichannel intraluminal impedance monitoring — the most comprehensive reflux test. Impedance detects ALL reflux events regardless of acidity (acid, weakly acidic, and non-acid/alkaline reflux). Measures reflux direction (proximal vs distal extent), bolus clearance, and symptom-reflux association. The test of choice for evaluating refractory GERD on PPI therapy and detecting non-acid reflux (bile, weakly acidic).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose refractory GERD on PPI; detect non-acid and weakly acidic reflux; evaluate bile reflux; extraesophageal GERD; correlate symptoms with reflux
diagnostic_tests.clinical_importance: Identifies the 40-50% of refractory GERD patients who continue to have symptoms from non-acid reflux despite adequate acid suppression — guides management beyond PPIs

diagnostic_tests.description: Measures LES pressure, esophageal peristaltic function, and coordination of swallowing. Uses a multi-sensor catheter (36 pressure sensors) generating a topographic pressure map (Clouse plot). Classifies motility disorders using Chicago Classification v4.0. MANDATORY before antireflux surgery to detect motility disorders (achalasia, absent contractility, severe hypomotility) that may contraindicate or modify surgical approach.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Evaluate LES pressure; detect esophageal motility disorders; mandatory pre-surgical evaluation; diagnosis of achalasia (important GERD mimic)
diagnostic_tests.key_metrics: LES IRP (integrated relaxation pressure), distal contractile integral (DCI), peristaltic break percentage; LES resting pressure; Chicago Classification diagnosis
diagnostic_tests.pre_surgical_importance: Absent contractility — fundoplication may worsen dysphagia; low LES pressure — favours surgery

diagnostic_tests.description: Wireless pH capsule clipped to the esophageal mucosa during endoscopy — records pH for 48-96 hours (vs 24 hours for catheter pH). Eliminates discomfort of nasal catheter, allows more normal diet and activity, extends monitoring period improving diagnostic yield. Particularly useful for patients with normal 24-hour pH monitoring but clinical suspicion of GERD.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Extended pH monitoring (48-96 hours) improving sensitivity; comfortable for patients; useful when catheter pH is negative but GERD strongly suspected
diagnostic_tests.advantage: Better patient tolerance; longer recording period; captures day-to-day variability in reflux

diagnostic_tests.description: Fluoroscopic examination of the esophagus and stomach after swallowing barium contrast. Provides structural assessment: hiatal hernia, esophageal stricture, esophageal dysmotility, and reflux (though sensitivity for detecting reflux is low). More useful for assessing anatomical abnormalities before surgery and evaluating dysphagia.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect hiatal hernia, esophageal stricture, motility disorders; evaluate dysphagia; pre-surgical anatomical assessment
diagnostic_tests.limitation: Low sensitivity for GERD diagnosis (~25-30%); cannot detect mucosal lesions or Barrett's; not a primary GERD diagnostic test

diagnostic_tests.description: Spectrophotometric fibre-optic probe detecting bilirubin (proxy for bile content) in esophageal aspirate. Used to quantify bile reflux in patients with suspected alkaline/bile reflux — particularly post-gastrectomy or post-surgical GERD.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect duodenogastroesophageal (bile) reflux in post-surgical patients and those with PPI-refractory GERD

diagnostic_tests.description: Patient consumes a radiolabelled meal; gamma camera measures gastric emptying rate over 4 hours. Standard gold standard for gastroparesis diagnosis. Identifies delayed gastric emptying contributing to GERD.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose gastroparesis contributing to GERD; guide use of prokinetics; evaluate refractory GERD
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Normal: >90% gastric emptying at 4 hours; Mild delay: 61-90% emptying; Moderate: 11-60%; Severe: <11% at 4 hours

diagnostic_tests.test_name: H. pylori Testing (Urea Breath Test / Stool Antigen)
diagnostic_tests.description: Helicobacter pylori testing should be performed in all patients with gastro-duodenal symptoms. H. pylori is a cause of gastric acid hypersecretion in some patients and contributes to peptic ulcer disease. Testing and treating H. pylori is part of standard upper GI workup. H. pylori eradication in GERD patients does NOT typically improve GERD symptoms.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude H. pylori as contributing cause of symptoms; mandatory in peptic ulcer disease; 'test and treat' strategy in dyspepsia
diagnostic_tests.when_to_test: All patients with upper GI symptoms; all patients with peptic ulcer; before long-term PPI (H. pylori may cause gastric atrophy on PPIs)

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Blood Tests (FBC, CRP, LFTs, Coeliac Screen, Calcium)
diagnostic_tests.description: Baseline blood investigations in GERD evaluation. Full blood count detects anaemia (iron-deficiency anaemia from occult GI bleeding — alarm feature). CRP (elevated in inflammatory conditions). Coeliac disease screen (anti-TTG antibodies) — coeliac can cause similar symptoms. Calcium: hypercalcaemia causes hypergastrinaemia and acid hypersecretion.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect anaemia (alarm feature); exclude coeliac disease; exclude Zollinger-Ellison (serum gastrin); assess nutritional status
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Iron-deficiency anaemia (low Hb, low ferritin, low MCV) in the context of GERD symptoms = URGENT ENDOSCOPY

diagnostic_tests.test_name: CT Scan of Chest and Abdomen
diagnostic_tests.description: Not a primary GERD diagnostic test. Used for: evaluating large hiatal hernia (para-oesophageal hernia — surgical planning); assessing extent of esophageal malignancy; unexplained chest symptoms.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Staging of suspected esophageal malignancy; evaluation of large/complicated hiatal hernia; unexplained chest or abdominal symptoms

medicines.note: GERD treatment follows a step-up or step-down approach. Lifestyle modification is the foundation of all GERD management. Medications are adjuncts, not replacements, for lifestyle changes. PPIs are the most effective pharmacological treatment. All medications should be prescribed by a licensed physician. Long-term PPI use requires periodic review and the lowest effective dose should be used.
treatment_goals: Achieve symptom relief and improve quality of life
Maintain remission with lowest effective treatment

categories.purpose: Rapidly neutralise gastric acid providing immediate (within minutes) but short-duration (30-90 minutes) relief of heartburn. Act by chemical neutralisation of acid — do not reduce acid production. Most effective when taken 1 hour after meals and at bedtime when symptoms peak. First choice for mild, infrequent heartburn.
categories.note: Antacids do NOT heal esophagitis, do NOT treat extraesophageal GERD, and are not sufficient for frequent or severe GERD. Overuse can cause diarrhoea (magnesium-based), constipation (aluminium-based), or milk-alkali syndrome (calcium carbonate excess).

medicines.name: Aluminium Hydroxide + Magnesium Hydroxide (co-magaldrox)
medicines.dosage: 10-20mL (liquid) or 2-4 chewable tablets 1 hour after meals and at bedtime; maximum 60mL/day
medicines.use_case: Immediate relief of mild to moderate heartburn; infrequent GERD symptoms
medicines.mechanism: Chemical neutralisation of gastric acid (Al(OH)3 + Mg(OH)2 neutralise HCl); magnesium reduces constipation caused by aluminium
side_effects: Constipation (aluminium excess — balanced in combination products)
Drug interactions: reduces absorption of tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, iron, digoxin — separate by 2 hours
medicines.note: Avoid long-term: aluminium toxicity risk in renal impairment; magnesium accumulation in renal failure

medicines.name: Calcium Carbonate
medicines.dosage: 500-1500mg as needed (1-3 tablets); maximum 7500mg/day
medicines.use_case: Mild, infrequent heartburn; convenient portable antacid
medicines.mechanism: Rapid neutralisation of gastric acid; also provides calcium supplementation
side_effects: Rebound acid hypersecretion (with very frequent use)
Milk-alkali syndrome (hypercalcaemia, alkalosis, renal impairment — with excessive long-term use)
medicines.note: Most rapid onset of all antacids; pleasant taste; convenient

medicines.name: Sodium Bicarbonate
medicines.dosage: 0.5-1 teaspoon in water as needed
medicines.use_case: Rapid emergency relief of acute heartburn; OTC use
medicines.mechanism: Rapid acid neutralisation with CO2 release
side_effects: Sodium load — avoid in hypertension, heart failure, oedema, pregnancy; avoid with sodium restriction
medicines.note: Fastest acting but shortest duration; significant sodium content limits frequent use

categories.purpose: Form a physical foam 'raft' on top of gastric contents that floats and physically displaces the acid pocket from the gastroesophageal junction, preventing reflux. Particularly effective for post-prandial heartburn and regurgitation. Mechanism is mechanical, not pharmacological — no systemic side effects. Ideal for pregnancy and mild GERD.

medicines.name: Sodium Alginate + Potassium Bicarbonate (Gaviscon)
medicines.dosage: 10-20mL liquid or 2-4 tablets after meals and at bedtime; maximum 4 doses per day; always after meals (raft forms in food-laden stomach)
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE for mild to moderate GERD; POST-PRANDIAL heartburn and regurgitation specifically; PREGNANCY (safest antireflux medication — not absorbed systemically); LPR/laryngopharyngeal reflux; add-on to PPI for breakthrough symptoms
medicines.mechanism: Alginate reacts with gastric acid to form a thick, cohesive gel raft (viscous alginate foam) that floats on the stomach contents — physical barrier preventing reflux of acid pocket into esophagus; separate from antacid neutralisation
side_effects: Essentially no systemic side effects (not absorbed)
Mild GI bloating in some patients
High sodium variants — avoid in fluid-restricted patients (low-sodium Gaviscon Advance available)
medicines.evidence: Cochrane review: alginates superior to placebo for GERD symptom relief; particularly effective for post-prandial and nocturnal reflux; comparable to H2 blockers for mild GERD

categories.purpose: Block histamine H2 receptors on gastric parietal cells, reducing acid secretion by approximately 70% at standard doses. Provide sustained acid suppression for 6-12 hours — better for overnight acid suppression than antacids. Less effective than PPIs (reduce acid by 70% vs PPIs by 95-99%). Still useful for mild-moderate GERD and on-demand treatment.
categories.note: Ranitidine (Zantac) was withdrawn globally in 2020 due to NDMA (N-nitrosodimethylamine) contamination concerns — carcinogenic impurity found on long-term storage. Famotidine and cimetidine are currently available H2RAs.

medicines.name: Famotidine
medicines.dosage: 20-40mg twice daily (before breakfast and bedtime) for GERD; 20mg OTC as needed (PRN); maximum 40mg twice daily
medicines.use_case: Mild to moderate GERD; nocturnal heartburn; step-down therapy after PPI induction; on-demand use; patients with mild symptoms not requiring PPI; add-on at bedtime for nocturnal symptoms even on PPIs
medicines.mechanism: Competitive reversible H2 receptor antagonist; reduces basal and meal-stimulated acid secretion; onset 30-45 min; duration 6-12 hours
side_effects: QT prolongation at very high doses (rare)
medicines.advantage_over_ppi: Rapid onset (30-45 min vs 60-90 min for PPI); effective for nocturnal acid breakthrough on PPIs (unique role — adding H2RA at bedtime reduces nocturnal acid breakthrough in PPI users); no proton pump activation required (unlike PPIs — effective even on empty stomach)

medicines.name: Cimetidine
medicines.dosage: 400-800mg twice daily or 400mg four times daily
medicines.use_case: Mild GERD; less commonly used than famotidine due to drug interactions
side_effects: Significant drug interactions — inhibits CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP2D6, CYP3A4 enzymes; interacts with warfarin, phenytoin, theophylline, amiodarone, metformin
Gynaecomastia and impotence (anti-androgenic effect with high doses)
medicines.note: Not recommended as first-choice H2RA due to extensive drug interactions; use famotidine instead

categories.category_name: Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs) — Gold Standard First-Line Treatment
categories.purpose: Irreversibly inhibit the H+/K+-ATPase (proton pump) in parietal cells — the final common pathway of acid secretion. Most potent acid suppressants available: reduce gastric acid by 95-99%. PPIs are the cornerstone of GERD pharmacotherapy — more effective than H2RAs for both symptom relief and mucosal healing. Standard-dose PPI once daily before breakfast heals >90% of erosive esophagitis within 8 weeks.
categories.critical_administration_note: PPIs must be taken 30-60 minutes BEFORE the first main meal (typically breakfast) to maximise efficacy. This is because PPIs only inhibit ACTIVE proton pumps — which are maximally activated by meal-stimulated acid secretion. Taking PPIs after meals or at bedtime (without a meal) significantly reduces their efficacy by 50-70%.

medicines.name: Omeprazole
medicines.form: Capsule, Tablet, Sachet for oral suspension, IV Infusion
medicines.dosage: Standard dose: 20mg once daily before breakfast; Double dose (severe/refractory): 20mg twice daily (before breakfast and dinner); Maintenance: 10-20mg once daily (lowest effective dose)
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE treatment for all GERD — erosive esophagitis, NERD, Barrett's esophagus, LPR; prevention and treatment of PPI-induced ulcers; Helicobacter pylori eradication triple therapy
medicines.mechanism: Pro-drug — absorbed in small intestine, activated by gastric acid, covalently and irreversibly binds H+/K+-ATPase (proton pump); inhibits acid secretion for 18-24 hours; new pumps synthesized each day (explaining daily dosing)
side_effects: GI: nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, constipation (common, usually mild)

Long-term side effects (clinically relevant with >1 year use): Hypomagnesaemia (can cause arrhythmia, tetany, seizures — monitor Mg2+ in long-term users); Vitamin B12 deficiency; C. difficile infection (increased risk); Community-acquired pneumonia (modest increase); Hip, wrist, and spine fractures (osteoporosis risk — controversial, especially at >1 year); Chronic kidney disease progression (controversial)

Drug interactions: reduces absorption of drugs requiring acid (ketoconazole, itraconazole, iron, clopidogrel); inhibits CYP2C19 (omeprazole and esomeprazole most — lansoprazole and pantoprazole least)
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to any PPI or benzimidazole
medicines.long_term_use_guidance: Review need annually; aim lowest effective dose; H. pylori test and treat before long-term PPI; supplement magnesium and vitamin B12 if using >1 year; prescribe calcium and Vitamin D if long-term use >3 years
medicines.note: Most prescribed medication in many countries; 5th most prescribed medication globally

medicines.name: Pantoprazole
medicines.dosage: Standard: 40mg once daily before breakfast; Double dose: 40mg twice daily; Maintenance: 20-40mg once daily
medicines.use_case: All GERD indications; PREFERRED in patients on antiplatelet therapy (least CYP2C19 interaction — does not reduce clopidogrel efficacy as much as omeprazole); IV pantoprazole for acute upper GI bleeding and critically ill patients
medicines.advantage: Lowest CYP2C19 drug interactions among PPIs; safe with clopidogrel; available IV
medicines.side_effects: Similar to omeprazole; headache more common than other PPIs

medicines.name: Rabeprazole
medicines.dosage: Standard: 20mg once daily before breakfast; Double: 20mg twice daily
medicines.use_case: All GERD indications; may have more rapid onset of acid suppression than other PPIs; less dependent on CYP2C19 metabolic pathway
medicines.advantage: Faster onset than other PPIs; less CYP2C19 dependent; useful in CYP2C19 rapid metabolisers who respond poorly to omeprazole/lansoprazole

medicines.name: Lansoprazole
medicines.dosage: Standard: 15-30mg once daily; Double: 30mg twice daily
medicines.use_case: All GERD indications; orodispersible (orally disintegrating) tablet useful in patients who cannot swallow capsules or for NG-tube administration
medicines.advantage: Orodispersible formulation (FasTabs) for patients with swallowing difficulty; can be mixed with water and given via NG-tube

medicines.name: Esomeprazole
medicines.dosage: Standard: 20-40mg once daily; Double: 40mg twice daily
medicines.use_case: All GERD indications; S-enantiomer of omeprazole with slightly superior acid suppression; commonly used for refractory GERD; available IV
medicines.advantage: S-enantiomer with slightly higher and more consistent acid suppression than omeprazole; popular for high-dose GERD management
medicines.note: More expensive than omeprazole with marginally superior efficacy — omeprazole remains first choice for cost-effectiveness

medicines.name: Dexlansoprazole
medicines.dosage: 30-60mg once daily (any time, not necessarily before meals)
medicines.use_case: All GERD indications, particularly nocturnal heartburn and refractory GERD; unique dual-release technology
medicines.mechanism: Dual delayed-release formulation — two release phases provide two peaks of plasma concentration (1 and 4-5 hours post-dose), providing more sustained acid suppression over 24 hours
medicines.advantage: Can be taken at any time of day (not meal-dependent unlike other PPIs); better nocturnal acid control; useful for patients who forget to take PPIs before meals

categories.category_name: Potassium-Competitive Acid Blockers (P-CABs) — Newer Potent Acid Suppressants
categories.purpose: Newest class of acid suppressants — reversibly and potassium-competitively block the H+/K+-ATPase (proton pump). Unlike PPIs: (1) work within 1-2 hours of first dose (vs PPIs requiring 3-5 days for maximum effect); (2) not pro-drug dependent (no activation required — work immediately); (3) more effective at controlling nocturnal acid; (4) not dependent on meal timing; (5) less affected by CYP2C19 polymorphisms (more predictable acid suppression across patients).

medicines.name: Vonoprazan
medicines.dosage: 20-40mg once daily; does not require meal-timing
medicines.use_case: Erosive esophagitis (superior healing rates vs PPIs in clinical trials); H. pylori eradication (dramatically improves eradication rates); refractory GERD; nocturnal GERD; Asian patients (potent regardless of CYP2C19 genotype)
medicines.mechanism: Potassium-competitive, reversible inhibition of H+/K+-ATPase — does not require activation; immediate onset; no meal timing requirement; more complete and consistent acid suppression
side_effects: Similar to PPIs: nausea, diarrhoea, abdominal pain
medicines.evidence: PURITY trials: vonoprazan 20mg superior to lansoprazole 15mg for healing erosive esophagitis at 2 and 4 weeks; FDA approved 2023 for erosive esophagitis and H. pylori eradication
medicines.availability: Approved in Japan (2015), USA (2023), and increasing globally; limited availability in some countries

categories.purpose: Accelerate gastric emptying and increase LES tone — addressing the motility component of GERD. Particularly useful when delayed gastric emptying, bloating, and regurgitation are prominent features. Generally used as adjuncts to PPIs, not monotherapy for GERD.

medicines.name: Metoclopramide
medicines.dosage: 10mg three times daily, 30 minutes before meals and at bedtime; maximum 5 days (oral); lower doses in elderly
medicines.use_case: GERD with gastroparesis; GERD with prominent nausea and bloating; short-term adjunct for regurgitation; antiemetic; not recommended for long-term GERD use
medicines.mechanism: D2 receptor antagonist (prokinetic) + 5-HT4 agonist — increases LES pressure; enhances gastric antral contractions; accelerates gastric emptying
side_effects: Extrapyramidal reactions (akathisia, dystonia) — common in young adults; AVOID in patients with Parkinson's disease
Tardive dyskinesia (irreversible — with long-term use; FDA black box warning)
medicines.black_box_warning: FDA black box warning: tardive dyskinesia risk with prolonged use (>12 weeks); limit to maximum 12 weeks

medicines.name: Domperidone
medicines.dosage: 10-20mg three times daily, 15-30 minutes before meals and at bedtime
medicines.use_case: GERD with delayed gastric emptying; nausea and vomiting; regurgitation; preferred prokinetic in many countries (UK, India, EU) due to fewer CNS side effects than metoclopramide (less blood-brain barrier penetration)
medicines.mechanism: Peripheral D2 receptor antagonist; increases LES pressure; accelerates gastric emptying; antiemetic (acts on chemoreceptor trigger zone)
side_effects: QT prolongation (cardiac monitoring in high-risk patients and elderly)
Minimal CNS effects (does not cross BBB readily)
contraindications: Cardiac disease with risk of QT prolongation

medicines.name: Mosapride Citrate
medicines.dosage: 2.5-5mg three times daily before meals
medicines.use_case: Gastroparesis; GERD with bloating and early satiety; widely used in Asia (Japan, India) for gastroparesis and GERD; fewer cardiac side effects than domperidone
medicines.mechanism: Selective 5-HT4 receptor agonist (no D2 antagonism); enhances gastric motility and gastric emptying; increases LES pressure
side_effects: No QT prolongation at standard doses
medicines.advantage: No QT prolongation risk; no dopaminergic side effects; safe in elderly

medicines.name: Itopride
medicines.dosage: 50mg three times daily before meals
medicines.use_case: Gastroparesis; functional dyspepsia with GERD overlap; bloating
medicines.mechanism: D2 receptor antagonist + acetylcholinesterase inhibitor — dual prokinetic mechanism; enhances acetylcholine-mediated gastric contractions

categories.purpose: Protect esophageal and gastric mucosa from acid injury through various mechanisms — coating, cytoprotection, or stimulation of mucosal defence mechanisms.

medicines.name: Sucralfate
medicines.dosage: 1g (10mL suspension or 2 × 500mg tablets) four times daily, 1 hour before meals and at bedtime
medicines.use_case: Peptic esophageal and gastric ulcers; adjunct for severe esophagitis; safe in pregnancy (category B — not absorbed); bile reflux (coats mucosa regardless of acidity)
medicines.mechanism: Polymerises in acidic environment (pH<3) to form viscous, gel-like coating on ulcerated mucosa; adsorbs bile salts and pepsin; stimulates prostaglandin synthesis and mucosal healing; acts as physical protective barrier
side_effects: Drug absorption interference — separate from other medications by at least 2 hours (adsorbs drugs)
medicines.administration: Must be taken on empty stomach; timing-critical; aluminium component — avoid in renal failure (aluminium accumulation)

medicines.name: Aloe Vera Juice (Pharmaceutical-Grade)
medicines.dosage: 10-15mL of standardised aloe vera juice before meals (pharmaceutical-grade — decolorised, purified)
medicines.use_case: Adjunctive soothing for esophagitis; anti-inflammatory; emerging evidence as gentle GERD adjunct
medicines.mechanism: Anti-inflammatory (reduces IL-8, TNF-α); antacid properties; mucosal coating
side_effects: GI upset with improperly prepared products
Electrolyte disturbances with latex-containing whole leaf (avoid — use inner leaf juice only)
medicines.evidence: Small RCT: aloe vera syrup reduced GERD symptoms comparable to omeprazole 20mg and ranitidine 150mg (limited evidence — adjunctive only)

categories.purpose: Reduces the frequency of Transient Lower Esophageal Sphincter Relaxations (TLESRs) — the primary mechanism of GERD. Acts centrally and peripherally on GABA-B receptors to reduce vagal TLESR-triggering signals from the stomach. Second-line for non-acid or refractory GERD on PPIs.

medicines.name: Baclofen
medicines.dosage: 5-25mg three times daily (start low — 5mg TDS; titrate up over weeks to reduce side effects)
medicines.use_case: Refractory GERD with documented weakly-acidic or non-acid reflux on pH-impedance; patients not responding to double-dose PPI; reduces reflux of all types (acid, weakly acid, bile); bile reflux
medicines.mechanism: GABA-B receptor agonist — inhibits TLESRs at the level of the brainstem dorsal motor nucleus and vagal afferents; reduces both acid and non-acid reflux events
side_effects: Significant CNS side effects: sedation, dizziness, cognitive impairment (dose-limiting)
Rebound symptoms on abrupt discontinuation — TAPER slowly
Risk of seizures on sudden withdrawal in high doses
medicines.clinical_role: Second or third-line agent; specialist-initiated; limited by CNS side effects; under evaluation with newer GABA-B agonists (lesogaberan — research stage)

categories.category_name: Neuromodulators — Functional Heartburn and Hypersensitive Esophagus
categories.purpose: Address central and peripheral sensitisation in patients with functional heartburn, hypersensitive esophagus, and visceral hypersensitivity — where standard acid suppression is insufficient or ineffective.

medicines.name: Amitriptyline (Low-Dose TCA)
medicines.dosage: 10-25mg at night (low dose — for visceral pain modulation; much lower than antidepressant doses of 75-150mg)
medicines.use_case: Functional heartburn; hypersensitive esophagus; refractory GERD with visceral hypersensitivity; esophageal spasm pain
medicines.mechanism: Reduces central and peripheral pain sensitisation (NMDA receptor modulation); reduces esophageal sensory afferent activity; improves sleep (beneficial in nocturnal GERD symptoms)
medicines.note: Low-dose TCA (10-25mg) is for neuromodulation, not antidepressant effect — explain clearly to patient

medicines.name: Citalopram / Sertraline (Low-Dose SSRI/SNRI)
medicines.dosage: Low-dose: citalopram 10-20mg daily; sertraline 25-50mg daily
medicines.use_case: Functional heartburn with comorbid anxiety or depression; hypersensitive esophagus; visceral hypersensitivity; refractory GERD with psychological overlay
medicines.mechanism: Serotonin reuptake inhibition — reduces esophageal hypersensitivity through 5-HT modulation; also treats comorbid anxiety (major contributor to functional heartburn)

categories.purpose: Definitive anatomical correction of the anti-reflux barrier for patients who prefer to avoid long-term medication, have refractory GERD, have large hiatal hernias, or have documented non-acid reflux not responsive to PPIs.
categories.note: Surgical candidacy requires thorough pre-operative evaluation: endoscopy (exclude Barrett's dysplasia), esophageal manometry (exclude achalasia/absent contractility), and ambulatory pH monitoring (confirm pathological acid exposure).

medicines.name: Laparoscopic Nissen Fundoplication (360° total fundoplication)
medicines.description: The surgical gold standard for GERD. The gastric fundus is wrapped 360° around the lower esophagus, reinforcing LES pressure and restoring anti-reflux barrier. Highly effective — 85-90% patient satisfaction at 5 years; comparative to PPI in RCTs (LOTUS trial).
medicines.use_case: Chronic GERD requiring long-term PPI; large hiatal hernia; refractory GERD with objective acid exposure; patient preference to avoid long-term medication; PPI side effects intolerable
complications: Gas bloat syndrome (10-20% — difficulty belching or vomiting)
Wrap slippage or breakdown (5-10% over 10 years — may require redo surgery)
medicines.outcomes: 85-90% symptom-free at 5-10 years; 50-60% still on PPI at 10 years (recurrent GERD or functional overlap)

medicines.name: Laparoscopic Toupet Fundoplication (270° partial posterior fundoplication)
medicines.description: Partial (270°) posterior wrap — less restrictive than Nissen. Preferred when esophageal motility is impaired (to reduce post-operative dysphagia risk). Lower dysphagia rate than Nissen; comparable acid control.
medicines.use_case: GERD with impaired esophageal motility (low-amplitude peristalsis); patients at high risk of post-operative dysphagia

medicines.name: LINX Magnetic Sphincter Augmentation (MSA)
medicines.description: Laparoscopically implanted titanium ring of magnetic beads placed around the LES. Magnetic attraction maintains LES closure; beads separate on swallowing (allowing food passage) or belching; naturally augments sphincter. Titanium implant — MRI-conditional (most modern MRI up to 1.5T safe).
medicines.use_case: Mild to moderate GERD with small or absent hiatal hernia; patients wishing to avoid PPI; seeking less invasive alternative to fundoplication; BMI <35
advantages: Preserves normal belching and vomiting ability (unlike Nissen)
complications: Inability to undergo high-field MRI after implant

medicines.name: Transoral Incisionless Fundoplication (TIF 2.0)
medicines.description: A scarless, incision-free fundoplication performed entirely through the mouth using a specialised endoscopic device (EsophyX or Medigus SRS). Creates a partial anterior fundoplication from inside. Suitable for patients with small hiatal hernia and moderate GERD.
medicines.use_case: Mild-moderate GERD without large hiatal hernia; patients with contraindications to conventional surgery or preferring less invasive option
medicines.advantages: No incision; faster recovery; reversible; can be combined with hiatal hernia repair (cTIF)
medicines.limitations: Less effective than laparoscopic fundoplication for severe GERD; not suitable for large hiatal hernias

medicines.name: Radiofrequency Ablation (Stretta Procedure)
medicines.description: Endoscopically delivered radiofrequency (RF) energy to the LES and gastric cardia — causes tissue remodelling, increases LES pressure, and may reduce TLESRs.
medicines.use_case: Mild-moderate GERD; patients not suitable for surgery; adjunct therapy
medicines.note: Modest evidence base; used in selected cases; less effective than surgical fundoplication

diet_and_nutrition.overview: Diet is the cornerstone of GERD management — dietary modifications are the most evidence-based non-pharmacological intervention. The primary goals are: (1) avoid foods that reduce LES pressure or increase acid secretion; (2) avoid foods that are directly acidic; (3) eat in a manner that minimises reflux risk (meal size, timing, position); (4) achieve and maintain healthy weight. Individual trigger foods vary — keeping a food diary identifying personal triggers is essential. A Mediterranean-style diet rich in vegetables, fish, and whole grains has been associated with lower GERD prevalence.

recommended_foods.evidence: Moderate — alkaline foods reduce gastric acidity; plant-based alkaline diet associated with lower GERD symptom frequency

items.benefit: Low in acid; high in soluble fibre (absorbs stomach acid; reduces reflux risk); filling without causing distension; slow gastric emptying in a positive way — thick consistency reduces reflux; gentle on esophageal mucosa. One of the best anti-reflux breakfast foods.
items.note: Add bananas, honey, or non-citrus fruit — avoid adding citrus or high-fat toppings

items.benefit: Natural antacid properties (alkaline pH ~4.6 — higher than most fruits); pectin coats stomach lining; high potassium reduces stomach acid; gentle on esophagus; easily digestible. One of the safest fruits for GERD.
Alkaline pH (7.5-8.0); high water content (dilutes gastric acid); non-acidic unlike most fruits; soothing to esophageal mucosa

Anti-inflammatory (reduces esophageal mucosal inflammation); prokinetic properties (mild gastric motility stimulant — promotes faster gastric emptying); anti-nausea; 6-gingerol reduces prostaglandin-mediated inflammation
items.frequency: Daily as tea or in cooking; 1-2cm fresh ginger in tea before meals

items.benefit: Small study evidence: high pH alkaline water (pH 8.8) permanently denatures pepsin (the proteolytic enzyme causing esophageal damage) — acid-activates pepsin which is the primary mucosal damage agent, not acid alone; alkaline water inactivates pepsin irreversibly
items.frequency: As primary hydration during and after meals

items.benefit: Low to moderate acidity; pectin; fibre; vitamins; tolerated by most GERD patients unlike citrus fruits
items.note: Some GERD patients may react to apple skin — try peeled apple first

items.benefit: Alkaline pH; healthy monounsaturated fats (do not reduce LES unlike saturated fats); anti-inflammatory; promotes satiety preventing overeating; rich in potassium
items.caution: Very high fat content — even healthy fats may delay gastric emptying; moderate portions

recommended_foods.evidence: Strong — vegetables are alkaline, low-fat, and form the basis of anti-GERD dietary patterns

items.food: Green leafy vegetables: Spinach, Kale, Lettuce, Bok choy, Green beans, Peas, Celery
items.benefit: Alkaline-forming foods; rich in Vitamin K, magnesium, calcium; low in fat; high in fibre; anti-inflammatory; associated with significantly lower GERD risk in dietary pattern studies

items.food: Root vegetables: Carrot, Sweet potato, Beetroot (non-pickled), Turnip
items.benefit: Alkaline pH; high fibre; filling; Vitamin A supports esophageal mucosal integrity; beta-carotene (antioxidant protective against Barrett's progression)
Low acid; anti-inflammatory; fibre; antioxidants including sulforaphane (broccoli) which may protect esophageal mucosa and reduce Barrett's risk; vitamin C
Anti-inflammatory; reduces gas and bloating (reduces distension-triggered TLESRs); fennel tea has mild antispasmodic properties; alkaline pH
items.frequency: Fennel tea after meals; fennel seeds to chew post-meal

items.food: Skinless chicken and turkey (baked, grilled, steamed — NOT fried)
items.benefit: Lean protein with low fat content (fat reduces LES pressure — lean meat avoids this); high satiety reduces overeating; neutral pH
items.cooking_method: Bake, grill, steam, or poach — NEVER fry (added fat worsens GERD)

items.food: White fish (cod, haddock, plaice, sole) and oily fish (salmon, mackerel — in moderation)
items.benefit: Lean protein; omega-3 anti-inflammatory properties (oily fish); low fat (white fish); anti-GERD diet staple
items.frequency: 3-4 times per week; oily fish 2 times per week

items.benefit: Pure lean protein without fat of yolk; easily digestible; neutral pH; filling
items.note: Egg yolks are high in fat — avoid or limit; egg whites are ideal

items.food: Legumes and lentils (dal, chickpeas, kidney beans)
items.benefit: Plant protein; high fibre; alkaline-forming; filling; low fat; associated with lower GERD risk
items.frequency: Daily in Indian diet context; excellent GERD-friendly protein source

items.food: Low-fat dairy: Skimmed milk, Low-fat yogurt (plain, unsweetened)
items.benefit: Protein and calcium; yogurt probiotics may improve gut motility; low-fat varieties do not reduce LES pressure (unlike full-fat dairy); cold milk provides very brief antacid effect (though rebound acid secretion follows full-fat milk)
items.frequency: Daily; low-fat or skimmed versions only
items.note: FULL-FAT dairy (full-fat milk, butter, cream, full-fat cheese) should be AVOIDED — fat content reduces LES pressure

items.food: Brown rice, Whole wheat bread (non-acidic), Whole wheat pasta, Quinoa
items.benefit: Complex carbohydrates; fibre reduces gastric acid concentration; low in fat; filling without causing distension; help maintain healthy weight (reduces GERD risk); neutral pH
Dilutes gastric acid; washes residual acid from esophagus; alkaline water inactivates pepsin; primary hydration of choice for GERD
items.frequency: 2-2.5 litres daily; sip consistently — avoid drinking large volumes at one time (distends stomach triggering TLESRs)

items.food: Herbal teas: Ginger tea, Chamomile tea, Licorice tea (deglycyrrhizinated), Slippery elm tea
items.benefit: Ginger: anti-inflammatory, prokinetic. Chamomile: anti-inflammatory, antispasmodic, reduces esophageal spasm. DGL Licorice: increases mucus production protecting esophageal mucosa (deglycyrrhizinated to remove hypertensive compound). Slippery elm: coats and soothes esophageal mucosa.
items.frequency: 2-3 cups daily; especially after meals and before bed
items.avoid: AVOID peppermint tea, spearmint tea — directly relax LES

items.benefit: Mildly alkaline (pH 5-7); electrolytes; hydrating; well-tolerated; reduces stomach acidity

items.food: Decolourised Aloe Vera inner leaf juice (pharmaceutical grade)
items.benefit: Anti-inflammatory; reduces esophageal mucosal inflammation; some antacid properties; emerging evidence as GERD adjunct (comparable to some medications in small RCTs)
items.frequency: 10-15mL before meals; only pharmaceutical-grade decolourised inner leaf juice (NOT whole leaf or latex-containing products)
items.caution: Avoid whole leaf aloe vera juice — contains anthraquinones (laxative effect, potentially carcinogenic with chronic use)

foods_to_avoid.reason: MOST IMPORTANT category to avoid. Fat reduces LES pressure via CCK (cholecystokinin) release; delays gastric emptying (increases volume and pressure for longer); the single most potent dietary trigger of GERD.
foods_to_avoid.mechanism: Dietary fat stimulates CCK release from duodenum → CCK activates vagal pathways → reduces LES pressure; TLESRs increase after fatty meals
examples: Full-fat dairy: cream, butter, full-fat cheese, whole milk
Red fatty meats (lamb, pork belly, fatty beef)
Pastries, croissants, pies (shortcrust and puff pastry)
Coconut oil and palm oil in large quantities

foods_to_avoid.reason: Directly relaxes LES smooth muscle; stimulates gastric acid secretion; promotes TLESRs
examples: Coffee — all types including espresso, cappuccino, instant
Green tea (in large amounts — some caffeine)

foods_to_avoid.reason: Triple mechanism: reduces LES pressure; stimulates gastric acid secretion; directly damages esophageal mucosa (alcohol-induced esophagitis); impairs esophageal peristalsis (reduces clearance); increases TLESRs
foods_to_avoid.note: Red wine has slightly less impact than beer on acid secretion but still causes significant reflux

foods_to_avoid.reason: L-menthol directly relaxes LES smooth muscle (L-type calcium channel dependent); despite perceived digestive benefits, mint is one of the most potent LES-relaxing foods. This COUNTERINTUITIVE fact surprises many patients.
examples: Peppermint tea (very commonly consumed as 'digestive aid' — paradoxically worsens GERD)
Mint-flavoured confectionery (after-dinner mints, mint chewing gum)
Toothpaste with high mint content (minimal relevance)

foods_to_avoid.reason: Contains methylxanthines (caffeine and theobromine — relax LES); high fat content (slows gastric emptying); stimulates acid secretion
examples: Dark chocolate (highest theobromine — worst for GERD despite being 'healthier')

foods_to_avoid.reason: Direct acid — lowers pH of gastric and esophageal contents; irritates already-inflamed esophageal mucosa; some fruits may also reduce LES pressure
foods_to_avoid.nuance: Whole fruit slightly better than juice (more fibre, less acid concentration); individually variable — some GERD patients tolerate small amounts of whole citrus

foods_to_avoid.reason: Highly acidic (pH 4.0-4.5); directly lowers gastric pH; tomato sauce concentrates acid during cooking; citric and malic acid content
CO2 gas directly and rapidly distends the stomach — the most potent immediate trigger for TLESRs; acidic pH of most sodas; caffeine in colas; phosphoric acid in some carbonated drinks
examples: All carbonated sodas (Coca-Cola, Pepsi, Sprite, Fanta)
Beer (also carbonated + acidic + alcohol — triple impact)

foods_to_avoid.reason: Capsaicin activates esophageal TRPV1 pain receptors (increases heartburn perception); delays gastric emptying; may directly injure inflamed esophageal mucosa; worsens symptoms without necessarily increasing acid production
High fermentable carbohydrate content causes gas production → gastric distension → TLESRs; raw form more problematic than cooked; FODMAPs trigger bloating and reflux in susceptible individuals
examples: Raw onion in salads or sandwiches
foods_to_avoid.note: Cooked onions and garlic much better tolerated than raw — cooking degrades fermentable carbohydrates

foods_to_avoid.reason: High in fat, salt, sugar, preservatives, and artificial additives — all promote inflammation and reduce esophageal mucosal integrity; promote obesity (biggest GERD risk factor); high glycaemic index promotes acid secretion

foods_to_avoid.food: Very hot or very cold foods and beverages
foods_to_avoid.reason: Thermal injury to esophageal mucosa; very hot beverages (>60°C) cause mucosal injury and are a risk factor for esophageal carcinoma; very cold foods cause esophageal spasm in sensitive individuals
examples: Very hot tea or coffee (allow to cool to <60°C before drinking)
Extremely cold foods immediately after warm food
foods_to_avoid.note: Allowing hot drinks to cool slightly (2-3 minutes) significantly reduces this risk

sample_meal_plan.note: This GERD-friendly low-acid, low-fat, high-fibre meal plan minimises reflux triggers while providing complete nutrition. Adjust based on individual trigger identification from food diary. Small, regular meals are key. Never eat large meals; do not lie down within 2-3 hours of eating.
sample_meal_plan.early_morning: 1 cup ginger tea or chamomile tea (warm, not hot) + soaked almonds (6-8) — before breakfast to coat stomach
sample_meal_plan.breakfast: Oatmeal/porridge with ripe banana and honey (no citrus) + 1 boiled egg white OR low-fat yogurt (plain, unsweetened) + glass of alkaline water
sample_meal_plan.mid_morning: Apple (peeled, red apple preferred) or pear OR melon slices + herbal fennel tea
sample_meal_plan.lunch: Grilled or baked chicken breast or steamed fish + brown rice or whole wheat chapati (2 — not 4) + cooked spinach or green beans with minimal oil + plain dal (moong/toor) + small cup of low-fat curd — moderate portion; do NOT overeat
sample_meal_plan.evening_snack: Oat biscuits or rice cakes + glass of water OR a small banana + 1 cup chamomile or DGL licorice tea
sample_meal_plan.dinner: Steamed or grilled fish or tofu + steamed broccoli and carrots + small portion of brown rice or 1-2 chapati — eat at least 3 hours before bedtime; small portion
sample_meal_plan.post_dinner: Ginger or chamomile herbal tea; 10-15mL aloe vera juice (pharmaceutical grade); DO NOT eat or lie down for minimum 2-3 hours
sample_meal_plan.before_bed: DO NOT eat or drink anything except small sips of water; elevate head of bed 15-20cm; sleep on LEFT SIDE

special_dietary_notes: MEAL SIZE is as important as WHAT you eat — large meals are a major TLESR trigger regardless of food type; eat 5-6 small meals per day rather than 3 large meals
DO NOT eat within 2-3 hours of bedtime — nocturnal acid exposure is particularly damaging (no saliva produced during sleep to neutralise acid; lying position promotes reflux)
Eat SLOWLY and chew thoroughly — rapid eating causes swallowing of air (aerophagia) which distends the stomach and triggers TLESRs; slow eating promotes better satiety with smaller portions

WEIGHT LOSS is the most powerful dietary intervention for GERD — even 5-10% body weight reduction (achievable through calorie restriction and Mediterranean diet) significantly reduces GERD frequency and severity
Mediterranean diet pattern strongly associated with lower GERD risk — high in vegetables, fish, olive oil (in moderation), legumes, and whole grains; low in red meat and processed foods
Keep a personalised FOOD DIARY for 4-6 weeks — note foods consumed, timing, and symptoms (1-3 hours later); identifies personal triggers that may differ from general guidelines
Avoid DRINKING large amounts WITH MEALS — small sips of water are fine but large volumes distend the stomach; drink water between meals
COOKING METHODS matter as much as food choice — baking, grilling, steaming, and poaching vs frying and sautéing in butter

weight_management.evidence: Strongest evidence base of any lifestyle intervention for GERD. Every 5-unit increase in BMI increases GERD odds by 35%; waist circumference >88cm (women) or >102cm (men) independently increases GERD risk. Even modest weight loss (5-10% body weight) reduces reflux frequency, improves symptoms, and can reduce or eliminate medication need.
weight_management.mechanisms: Weight loss: reduces intra-abdominal pressure; reduces hiatal hernia size; reduces transient LES relaxations; improves gastric emptying
weight_management.targets: BMI <25 kg/m²; waist circumference <80cm (women) or <94cm (men); 5-10% body weight loss for symptomatic improvement
strategies: Structured weight loss programme with dietitian
Consider bariatric surgery for BMI >35 with GERD — Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (improves GERD); sleeve gastrectomy (may worsen GERD — important counselling point)

head_of_bed_elevation.description: Elevating the head of the bed 15-20 cm (6-8 inches) uses gravity to prevent nocturnal acid reflux during sleep. Reduces the time acid remains in contact with the esophageal mucosa overnight. Using extra pillows alone is INSUFFICIENT — pillows fold and lose height during sleep; also cause neck strain.
head_of_bed_elevation.method: Place solid bed risers under the head end of the bed frame; or use a purpose-made wedge pillow (foam wedge under mattress — 20-25cm rise); or purchase an adjustable anti-reflux pillow
head_of_bed_elevation.evidence: Multiple RCTs show 25-30% reduction in esophageal acid exposure with head elevation; significantly reduces nocturnal symptom frequency
head_of_bed_elevation.note: Most effective when combined with other lifestyle measures; critical for patients with nocturnal GERD symptoms and LPR

left_lateral_position.description: Sleeping on the LEFT side significantly reduces nocturnal acid reflux compared to right lateral or supine position. The gastroesophageal junction is positioned above the stomach contents when lying on the left, using gravity to keep stomach contents in the fundus.
left_lateral_position.mechanism: Left lateral decubitus: GEJ is superior to stomach acid pool; acid pool pooled in fundus (away from GEJ). Right lateral decubitus: GEJ is inferior to acid pool — promotes acid contact with GEJ
left_lateral_position.evidence: pH studies demonstrate significantly lower esophageal acid exposure in left lateral vs right lateral or supine position

meal_timing.description: DO NOT eat for at least 2-3 hours before lying down or going to bed. Allow gastric emptying before assuming horizontal position. This is consistently among the most effective lifestyle measures for reducing nocturnal GERD.
meal_timing.target: Last meal at least 3 hours before bedtime; last snack at least 2 hours before bedtime

exercise_and_physical_activity.overview: Regular moderate-intensity exercise reduces GERD by promoting weight loss, improving gut motility, and reducing abdominal fat. However, certain types of high-intensity exercise can PROVOKE or WORSEN reflux.
beneficial: Brisk walking — 30-45 min daily; reduces weight; improves gut motility without provoking reflux
Cycling (moderate pace) — non-impact; good for weight loss without abdominal pressure
Swimming — horizontal but head elevation in water differs from bed; generally well-tolerated
Yoga (avoiding head-down and abdominal compression poses) — reduces stress, improves gut-brain axis
Light resistance training — standing exercises; improves metabolism and weight loss
avoid_or_modify: High-impact activities immediately after eating — running, jumping — increase intra-abdominal pressure; wait 2+ hours after meals
Inverted yoga poses (headstand, downward dog with head below stomach) — gravity reversal promotes reflux
Heavy abdominal crunches and sit-ups — increase intra-abdominal pressure
