Exercises requiring bending at the waist immediately post-meal
Marathon running — sustained impact increases reflux; exercise-induced GERD common in long-distance runners
exercise_and_physical_activity.timing: Exercise 2-3 hours after meals; stay well-hydrated; avoid caffeinated sports drinks

smoking_cessation.evidence: Smoking is a significant modifiable risk factor for GERD. Mechanisms: reduces LES pressure; impairs salivary bicarbonate secretion (salivary bicarbonate is a natural esophageal acid neutraliser); stimulates gastric acid secretion; impairs esophageal peristalsis (reduces clearance efficiency). Smokers have longer esophageal acid exposure times and higher rates of Barrett's esophagus.
smoking_cessation.benefit_of_cessation: LES pressure improves within weeks of cessation; salivary bicarbonate secretion normalises; overall GERD improvement
smoking_cessation.resources: NRT (patches, gum, lozenges), varenicline (Champix), bupropion; NHS Stop Smoking services; apps (Smoke Free, Quit Now)

alcohol_reduction.evidence: All alcohol worsens GERD — reduces LES pressure, stimulates acid, damages mucosa, impairs peristalsis. Beer is particularly problematic (acidic + carbonated + alcohol). Reducing or eliminating alcohol is a priority lifestyle modification.
alcohol_reduction.recommendation: Ideally eliminate alcohol; if consumed, limit to small amounts (≤1 unit/day); avoid wine, beer, and spirits particularly close to bedtime; never drink alcohol before lying down

clothing_and_posture: Wear loose-fitting clothing — avoid tight waistbands, belts, corsets, and shapewear that compress the abdomen and increase intragastric pressure
Maintain upright posture after meals — sit upright for at least 2-3 hours post-meal; avoid slouching forward (increases intra-abdominal pressure)
Avoid prolonged bending at the waist immediately after meals

stress_management.importance: Psychological stress is a significant contributor to GERD through multiple mechanisms: increases gastric acid secretion (cortisol and stress hormones); heightens esophageal visceral sensitivity (same mechanisms as in IBS); worsens symptoms even without increasing actual acid reflux volume (central sensitisation); impairs immune mucosal defense. Anxiety and depression are highly prevalent in refractory GERD patients.
techniques: Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) — strongest evidence for functional GI disorders including GERD; addresses catastrophising, anxiety-driven symptom amplification
Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) — reduces stress-mediated symptom amplification
Diaphragmatic breathing exercises — reduces intra-abdominal pressure; vagal tone enhancement; reduces TLESRs when practiced regularly (emerging evidence); 10-15 minutes twice daily
Gut-directed hypnotherapy — evidence for functional heartburn and refractory GERD
Regular yoga and meditation — reduces stress, improves gut-brain axis
Adequate sleep — sleep deprivation worsens GERD through increased acid sensitivity and stress response

medication_review: Review ALL medications regularly with GP for possible GERD-causing drugs: NSAIDs, calcium channel blockers, nitrates, bisphosphonates, anticholinergics, theophylline — switch to alternatives where possible
When NSAIDs are unavoidable: switch to paracetamol for pain where possible; if NSAID required, add gastroprotective PPI concomitantly
Bisphosphonates: take strictly with large volume of water; remain upright for 30 minutes; consider IV bisphosphonate or weekly/monthly formulations if daily tablet causes esophagitis
Antibiotics: doxycycline, tetracycline, clindamycin — take with large volume of water in upright position; do NOT take at bedtime without remaining upright
Hormone replacement therapy: route and type of HRT may affect GERD — discuss with prescriber
meal_habits: Eat slowly and mindfully — aim for 20-30 minutes per meal; chewing thoroughly reduces air swallowing and improves digestion
5-6 small meals per day rather than 3 large ones — smaller gastric volume reduces distension and TLESRs
Eat sitting upright — avoid eating while lying down, in bed, or while reclining
Do not eat while emotionally stressed or rushed — autonomic nervous system in 'fight or flight' diverts from digestion
Avoid talking excessively while eating — increases air swallowing (aerophagia)
Last meal should be the lightest of the day — avoid large, heavy dinners; avoid eating within 3 hours of bedtime
Chew sugarless gum after meals (non-mint flavoured) — stimulates salivary bicarbonate production which neutralises esophageal acid and reduces post-prandial reflux duration (evidence-based)

gerd_monitoring_plan.note: GERD monitoring tracks symptom frequency and severity, medication response, alarm feature development, and complication surveillance. The GERD-Health-Related Quality of Life (GERD-HRQL) questionnaire or the Reflux Disease Questionnaire (RDQ) can quantify symptom burden before and after treatment.

green_zone.criteria: Heartburn and regurgitation ≤1 day/week on or off medication; no dysphagia; no alarm symptoms; no nocturnal symptoms; quality of life not significantly impaired; on lowest effective dose of medication (or symptom-free on lifestyle changes alone)
green_zone.action: Continue current regimen. Annual review to reassess medication need (attempt step-down to lowest effective dose or on-demand therapy). Continue lifestyle modifications. If on long-term PPI: annual review of indication; monitor magnesium and B12 annually if on PPI >1 year. Barrett's surveillance as scheduled if applicable.

yellow_zone.criteria: Heartburn/regurgitation 2-4 days per week on current medication; nocturnal symptoms disturbing sleep; required antacids/alginates breakthrough >2x per week; symptoms impacting daily activities; increasing food restrictions to control symptoms
yellow_zone.action: Contact GP or gastroenterologist within 2-4 weeks. Reassess medication: optimise PPI timing (30-60 min before meals); consider dose increase to twice daily; add alginate (Gaviscon) for breakthrough; add bedtime H2 blocker (famotidine) for nocturnal symptoms. Reinforce lifestyle modifications. Referral for endoscopy if not done recently or if symptoms changed in character.

red_zone.status: URGENT — Alarm Features or Severe Complications
red_zone.criteria: Any of: new or progressive dysphagia (difficulty swallowing); odynophagia (painful swallowing); unexplained significant weight loss (>5%); haematemesis (vomiting blood) or melaena (tarry stools); iron-deficiency anaemia detected on bloods; persistent vomiting; new onset symptoms after age 55; GERD symptoms completely unresponsive after 8 weeks of full-dose PPI
red_zone.action: URGENT endoscopy referral within 2 weeks (2-week wait urgent referral for suspected upper GI cancer in most health systems). In case of active GI bleeding (haematemesis, melaena with haemodynamic instability) — EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT IMMEDIATELY. Do not delay alarm feature investigation with further empirical treatment changes.

complications.description: Progressive acid-induced mucosal erosions involving >50% of the esophageal circumference (Grade C) or ≥75% circumference (Grade D). Associated with significant mucosal damage, pain, bleeding, and high risk of stricture and Barrett's. Found in 30-40% of endoscoped GERD patients.
complications.management: High-dose PPI (twice daily); repeat endoscopy at 8 weeks to confirm healing; long-term maintenance PPI; surgical evaluation if recurrent
complications.note: Grade D esophagitis heals completely in >95% with 8-week high-dose PPI therapy

complications.description: Fibrous cicatricial narrowing of the distal esophagus from chronic acid-induced injury and healing. Presents with progressive dysphagia (initially for solids, eventually for soft foods and liquids). Most common benign cause of esophageal stricture. Found in 10-15% of patients with erosive esophagitis.
complications.management: Urgent endoscopy (exclude malignancy — biopsy of stricture mandatory); endoscopic balloon or bougie dilatation (usually requires 2-4 sessions); long-term high-dose PPI to prevent recurrence; surgical fundoplication reduces stricture recurrence
complications.note: After dilatation, 75% require repeat dilatation within 2 years without acid suppression; PPI reduces this significantly

complications.description: Pre-malignant change of distal esophageal squamous epithelium to intestinal-type columnar metaplasia (with goblet cells) — the body's maladaptive response to chronic acid injury. The single most important GERD complication. Prevalence in chronic GERD patients: 10-15%. Identified on endoscopy with salmon-pink tongues of mucosa extending into the tubular esophagus above the GEJ (confirmed by Prague C and M criteria for length measurement; confirmed by biopsy showing goblet cells).
complications.management: High-dose PPI (acid suppression associated with reduced progression risk); structured surveillance endoscopy programme; endoscopic eradication therapy (RFA, EMR, cryotherapy) for dysplastic Barrett's per guidelines
complications.surveillance: No dysplasia: every 3-5 years (BSG/ACG); indefinite low-grade dysplasia: endoscopic eradication or surveillance every 6-12 months; high-grade dysplasia: endoscopic eradication therapy

complications.description: The most serious GERD complication — a cancer with one of the fastest rising incidence rates in Western countries. Develops from high-grade dysplastic Barrett's esophagus. Risk factors: male sex, chronic GERD (>5 years), Barrett's esophagus, obesity, smoking, and Caucasian ethnicity. Typically presents late (dysphagia, weight loss) — carries poor prognosis (5-year survival ~20% for symptomatic presentation; >80% for early detection via surveillance).
complications.management: Multi-disciplinary team approach; staging CT and PET-CT; endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) or submucosal dissection (ESD) for T1 mucosal cancer; esophagectomy; chemoradiotherapy; palliative treatment for advanced disease
complications.prevention: Barrett's surveillance programme is the primary prevention strategy; smoking cessation; weight management; aspirin use may reduce progression (ongoing trials)

complications.description: Nocturnal aspiration of refluxate into the tracheobronchial tree causes recurrent aspiration pneumonia, aspiration pneumonitis, pulmonary fibrosis, and worsening of asthma and COPD. More common with hiatal hernia, elderly, and neurological disorders impairing the cough reflex.
complications.management: Aggressive GERD treatment (PPI); head elevation; prokinetics to improve gastric emptying; consider surgical antireflux procedure for refractory aspiration

complications.description: Chronic acid contact with the larynx causes: contact ulcers (granulomas on vocal cords), subglottic stenosis, posterior laryngitis, laryngeal carcinoma (increased risk with chronic acid exposure), vocal cord nodules, recurrent laryngitis.
complications.severity: Moderate — chronic voice changes; rare laryngeal malignancy risk
complications.management: High-dose twice-daily PPI; ENT/laryngology assessment; voice therapy; lifestyle modifications (head elevation, diet)

complications.description: Acid contact with teeth during regurgitation episodes causes irreversible erosion of dental enamel — particularly on the palatal surfaces of maxillary incisors and upper premolars (sites of acid pooling). GERD is the most common cause of erosive tooth wear in adults. Often first detected by dentists.
complications.management: GERD treatment; dental fluoride applications; use of straw for acidic drinks to reduce tooth contact; rinse mouth with water after reflux episodes (do not brush immediately — acid-softened enamel is more vulnerable to abrasion); custom tooth-protective fluoride trays

complications.description: Chronic acid exposure damages the smooth muscle and myenteric plexus of the esophagus, impairing peristaltic function. This creates a vicious cycle: impaired peristalsis reduces acid clearance, worsening GERD, causing more dysmotility. Manifests as low-amplitude esophageal contractions on manometry.
complications.management: Effective acid suppression halts progression; prokinetics; fundoplication consideration when associated with large hiatal hernia

complications.description: Nocturnal reflux is particularly damaging because: lying position promotes acid pooling in the esophagus; swallowing frequency reduces (less acid clearance); salivary bicarbonate secretion stops during sleep. Leads to chronic sleep deprivation, impaired quality of life, fatigue, and anxiety — creating a vicious cycle with GERD worsening.
complications.severity: Moderate — significant quality of life impact
complications.management: Alginate at bedtime; bedtime H2 blocker (famotidine) added to morning PPI; head of bed elevation; left lateral sleeping position; dexlansoprazole (better nocturnal acid control)

key_points: GERD affects 30-80% of pregnant women — the most common GI complaint in pregnancy; highest prevalence in 3rd trimester (75-80%)
Mechanisms: progesterone reduces LES pressure (smooth muscle relaxation); oestrogen increases gastric acid secretion; mechanical compression by enlarging uterus increases intra-abdominal pressure
Typically resolves postpartum; rarely requires investigation during pregnancy (avoid endoscopy in 1st trimester and avoid radiation)
SAFE medications in pregnancy (step-up approach):
Step 1 (First-line): Lifestyle modifications + Gaviscon (alginate) — sodium alginate is not absorbed; no systemic effects; SAFE all trimesters
Step 2: Antacids — calcium carbonate (Tums, Rennie) and magnesium hydroxide (NOT aluminium antacids — aluminium potentially neurotoxic to fetus in high doses); SAFE short-term
Step 3: H2 blockers — Famotidine is preferred; category B safety; use if antacids/alginates insufficient

Step 4: PPIs — Omeprazole and lansoprazole considered safe in pregnancy (observational data from registries; no increased congenital malformations); use when H2 blockers insufficient; 2nd and 3rd trimester preferred
AVOID in pregnancy: Sodium bicarbonate (high sodium load; alkalosis risk); prokinetics (metoclopramide — use with caution; dopamine effects in fetus); misoprostol
BACLOFEN and surgery: absolutely avoid during pregnancy
GER (physiological reflux) affects up to 50% of infants under 3 months — normal and self-limiting; due to immature LES, horizontal posture, liquid diet; 'happy spitters' with normal growth
GERD (pathological reflux disease) in infants: failure to thrive, food refusal, arching, persistent crying, sleep disturbance, recurrent apnoea — requires investigation and treatment

Interventions for infant GER/GERD: feed thickener (rice cereal or commercial thickener — reduces regurgitation); smaller, more frequent feeds; prone position DURING AWAKE SUPERVISED time (back-sleeping remains mandatory for unsupervised sleep — SIDS risk); maternal dietary modification if breastfeeding (reduce dairy if cow's milk protein intolerance suspected)

Pharmacological: alginate (Gaviscon Infant — special infant formulation) — first pharmacological choice; H2 blockers (famotidine — licensed for infants ≥1 month); PPIs (omeprazole — licensed from birth for severe GERD; lansoprazole from ≥1 year)
Older children (>12 years): managed similarly to adults; standard PPI doses
Paediatric GERD rarely needs antireflux surgery; most improve with age as LES matures
Fundoplication in children: considered for life-threatening complications (aspiration, severe failure to thrive) or neurologically impaired children with refractory GERD
GERD presentations in elderly are frequently atypical — chest pain may be cardiac-like; dysphagia may be attributed to normal aging; extraesophageal symptoms (cough, voice changes) common
Higher prevalence of complications: more likely to have erosive esophagitis, peptic strictures, and Barrett's — longer disease duration; reduced esophageal mucosal defense
Polypharmacy — many GERD-causing drugs more prevalent in elderly (CCBs, nitrates, anticholinergics, NSAIDs, bisphosphonates); medication review is critical
PPI safety concerns in elderly: higher risk of C. difficile, pneumonia, hip fractures, and hypomagnesaemia — use lowest effective dose; annual review
H2 blockers (cimetidine — AVOID in elderly; significant drug interactions and CNS effects including confusion — use famotidine instead)
Reduced peristaltic amplitude in elderly impairs acid clearance — head of bed elevation and meal timing particularly important
Prokinetics in elderly: metoclopramide — avoid (higher extrapyramidal and tardive dyskinesia risk); domperidone with caution (QT prolongation risk); mosapride preferred
Aspiration risk higher in elderly — aggressive treatment of nocturnal GERD; aspiration precautions
All patients with confirmed Barrett's esophagus should be on high-dose PPI indefinitely (acid suppression is associated with reduced risk of dysplasia progression)

Aspirin 300mg daily — considered for Barrett's patients at higher cancer risk (male, older, long-segment, dysplasia) — cardioprotective benefit and emerging evidence for chemoprevention (ongoing AspECT trial data supports cancer risk reduction)
Structured surveillance endoscopy programme — intervals determined by presence and grade of dysplasia (see Barrett's type section)
Lifestyle: weight loss, smoking cessation, alcohol reduction — all reduce Barrett's cancer progression risk

Endoscopic eradication therapy: radiofrequency ablation (RFA) is first-line for dysplastic Barrett's — ablates columnar epithelium allowing regeneration of normal squamous mucosa with continued PPI therapy; 90% effective for high-grade dysplasia
MDT discussion for all dysplastic Barrett's: gastroenterology, upper GI surgery, clinical oncology, histopathology — joint decision on endoscopic vs surgical management
GERD and OSA have a bidirectional relationship — OSA increases GERD; GERD worsens OSA
Mechanism: negative intrathoracic pressure during obstructive apnoeas promotes reflux; CPAP use in OSA has been shown to reduce reflux in some patients
CPAP therapy for OSA should be prescribed; patients should also receive optimised GERD treatment
Nocturnal GERD management is particularly important in this group

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Influenza respiratory illness causes severe coughing — increased cough and Valsalva efforts dramatically worsen GERD symptoms and reflux episodes. Influenza-associated pneumonia is more dangerous in patients with GERD-related aspiration risk. Annual vaccination recommended for all GERD patients on long-term PPIs (PPIs increase infection susceptibility slightly).

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: Per national schedule; single dose or 2-dose series depending on age and risk
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Long-term PPI use is associated with modestly increased risk of community-acquired pneumonia (reduced gastric acid allows bacteria to survive and potentially aspirate). Patients with GERD-related aspiration and those on long-term PPIs have increased pneumococcal pneumonia risk. Pneumococcal vaccination recommended for all adults on long-term PPIs.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is GERD and what causes it?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: GERD (Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease) is a chronic condition where stomach acid flows back (refluxes) into the esophagus because the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) — the valve between the stomach and esophagus — fails to work properly. The most common mechanism is 'transient LES relaxations' — inappropriate, brief openings of the valve that allow acid to escape. Contributing factors include hiatal hernia (stomach slipping above the diaphragm), obesity, pregnancy, certain foods (fatty foods, caffeine, chocolate, mint, alcohol), smoking, specific medications (NSAIDs, calcium channel blockers), and delayed gastric emptying.

frequently_asked_questions.question: How do I know if I have GERD or just occasional heartburn?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Everyone experiences heartburn occasionally — this is normal. GERD is diagnosed when heartburn or regurgitation occurs at least 2 days per week for more than 4-8 weeks AND causes troublesome symptoms or complications. The Montréal Consensus definition: heartburn or regurgitation that is 'troublesome' to the patient (impacts quality of life, affects eating, sleeping, or daily activities). If symptoms are frequent, waking you at night, not relieved by antacids, or accompanied by difficulty swallowing or weight loss — you have GERD requiring medical evaluation.

frequently_asked_questions.question: When should I take a PPI and how long should I take it?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Timing is critical for PPI effectiveness: take your PPI 30-60 minutes BEFORE your first main meal of the day (breakfast). PPIs only work on actively pumping proton pumps — which are maximally activated by food. Taking PPIs after meals or at bedtime reduces their efficacy by 50-70%. For acute symptom healing: 4-8 weeks of standard dose. For maintenance: lowest effective dose (discuss with doctor after 8-week course). Some patients need ongoing maintenance therapy; others can step down to on-demand use. Review PPI need annually with your doctor — use the lowest dose that controls symptoms.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Are PPIs safe for long-term use?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Standard-dose PPIs are safe for most patients in the short and medium term. Long-term use (>1-3 years) is associated with modest risks: hypomagnesaemia (low magnesium — monitor levels if taking >1 year; supplement if low); Vitamin B12 deficiency (reduce absorption — supplement if needed); slightly increased Clostridium difficile infection risk; modest increased fracture risk (controversial — magnitude uncertain); slightly higher community-acquired pneumonia risk. HOWEVER: for patients with confirmed erosive esophagitis, Barrett's esophagus, or significant complications, the benefits of long-term PPI far outweigh these small risks. The key principle: use the lowest effective dose for the shortest required duration. Review annually.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is Barrett's esophagus and should I be worried?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Barrett's esophagus is a pre-malignant change in the esophageal lining — the normal squamous cells are replaced by intestinal-type cells (columnar metaplasia) as an adaptive response to chronic acid injury. It occurs in about 10-15% of patients with long-term GERD. Barrett's IS a risk factor for esophageal adenocarcinoma — but the absolute annual risk is low (~0.3% per year without dysplasia). The important thing is: once diagnosed, follow your gastroenterologist's surveillance schedule (repeat endoscopy every 3-5 years); take high-dose PPI; make lifestyle changes; and if dysplasia is found, discuss endoscopic treatment (radiofrequency ablation — very effective). Most people with Barrett's never develop cancer.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can GERD cause asthma or chronic cough?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes — GERD is one of the most common causes of chronic cough (accounting for 20-40% of cases) and can trigger or worsen asthma. This is called 'extraesophageal GERD' or Laryngopharyngeal Reflux (LPR). Mechanisms: refluxate reaching the larynx and trachea triggers a vagal cough reflex; micro-aspiration of acid particles into the airways causes bronchospasm; acid can also stimulate esophageal-bronchial reflexes triggering cough and bronchospasm without actual aspiration. The paradox: many patients with GERD-related cough have no heartburn at all — it's 'silent reflux'. Twice-daily PPI for 8-12 weeks is the diagnostic and therapeutic approach.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What are the most important lifestyle changes for GERD?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Evidence-based GERD lifestyle changes (most to least important): (1) Weight loss — the most impactful change; even 5-10% body weight reduction significantly reduces symptoms; (2) Elevate head of bed 15-20cm (not just a pillow — use bed risers or a wedge under the mattress); (3) Do not eat within 2-3 hours of bedtime; (4) Sleep on your left side; (5) Avoid trigger foods: fatty foods, caffeine, alcohol, chocolate, mint, citrus, tomatoes, carbonated drinks; (6) Eat smaller more frequent meals; (7) Stop smoking; (8) Wear loose clothing; (9) Chew non-mint sugar-free gum after meals (stimulates saliva which neutralises acid).

frequently_asked_questions.question: Why does peppermint tea make my GERD worse?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: This surprises most people — peppermint is widely promoted as a 'digestive aid' but actually WORSENS GERD. The menthol in peppermint directly relaxes the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) muscle by blocking calcium channels in the muscle cells. A relaxed LES allows stomach acid to reflux into the esophagus more easily. So peppermint tea, peppermint sweets, mint chewing gum, and peppermint oil supplements — despite their pleasant digestive sensation — all worsen GERD. Replace peppermint tea with ginger tea or chamomile tea — both actually IMPROVE GERD symptoms.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is GERD related to stress and anxiety?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes, significantly. Psychological stress worsens GERD through multiple mechanisms: (1) Stress hormones increase gastric acid secretion; (2) Stress heightens esophageal sensory sensitivity — the same amount of acid reflux feels more painful when stressed; (3) Stress impairs esophageal mucosal defense mechanisms; (4) Anxiety promotes hypervigilance to normal GI sensations. This explains why GERD often worsens during stressful life events. For patients with 'functional heartburn' (symptoms without actual excess acid), psychological factors are the primary driver — where CBT and stress management are more effective than PPIs.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the difference between GERD, heartburn, acid reflux, and indigestion?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Heartburn is a SYMPTOM — the burning sensation in the chest. Acid reflux describes the PHYSICAL EVENT — stomach acid backing up into the esophagus. GERD is the DISEASE — a chronic condition of pathological acid reflux causing troublesome symptoms or complications. Indigestion (dyspepsia) is a broader term covering upper abdominal discomfort, bloating, and nausea — may or may not involve acid reflux; has significant overlap with GERD. In summary: you experience heartburn when acid reflux occurs; when this happens frequently enough to be a medical problem, you have GERD.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can GERD be cured with surgery?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Antireflux surgery — most commonly laparoscopic Nissen fundoplication — can provide durable long-term cure for GERD in appropriately selected patients. The gastric fundus is wrapped around the lower esophagus to reinforce the LES. Clinical trials (LOTUS) show surgery and PPIs have equivalent outcomes at 5 years. Key points: surgery is most effective for documented pathological acid reflux with good response to PPIs (if PPIs don't work, surgery often doesn't either for symptom relief); esophageal motility must be tested before surgery; 85-90% patient satisfaction at 5-10 years; side effects include bloating, gas, and difficulty belching in 10-20% of patients. It's a valid option for those seeking freedom from long-term medication or those with refractory non-acid reflux.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What foods should I definitely avoid with GERD?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: The most evidence-based foods to avoid: (1) Fatty and fried foods — most important trigger; reduce LES pressure significantly; (2) Alcohol — triple mechanism (LES relaxation, acid stimulation, mucosal injury); (3) Peppermint — directly relaxes LES; (4) Caffeine — coffee, strong tea, energy drinks; (5) Chocolate — methylxanthines relax LES; (6) Carbonated beverages — gas immediately triggers TLESRs; (7) Citrus fruits and tomatoes — acid content worsens mucosal injury; (8) Spicy foods — activate TRPV1 pain receptors. Individual triggers vary — keep a food diary to identify YOUR personal triggers.

frequently_asked_questions.question: I have GERD and chest pain. Could it be heart disease?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: CARDIAC CHEST PAIN MUST ALWAYS BE EXCLUDED FIRST. GERD is the most common non-cardiac cause of chest pain (responsible for 20-30% of non-cardiac chest pain presentations), but it can be absolutely indistinguishable from cardiac angina — both cause substernal chest discomfort that may radiate to the jaw or arm. RED FLAGS requiring immediate emergency assessment: chest pain with breathlessness, sweating, radiation down the left arm, occurring at rest or on exertion, in a person with risk factors (smoking, high blood pressure, diabetes, family history of heart disease, age >50). Never assume chest pain is 'just GERD' without cardiac evaluation. Once cardiac causes are excluded, a positive PPI trial (relief of symptoms on omeprazole 20mg twice daily for 2 weeks) supports GERD as the cause.
